It lies in the closed interval [0, 1].
questions.explanation: Within T, belonging to (0, 1) implies rationality. Taking the contrapositive, not being rational implies not belonging to (0, 1). An irrational member could be negative or greater than 1.

questions.stem: If a figure is both open and bounded, it has property S. Which statement is logically equivalent?
options: If it is closed then it lacks S.
If it has S then it is open.
If it lacks S then it is not open or not bounded.
If it lacks S then it is neither open nor bounded.
If it is not bounded then it lacks S.
questions.explanation: The negation of the conjunction is the disjunction of the negations. Only one of the two properties needs to fail.

questions.stem: Which statement follows the contrapositive rule for ‘If n is a multiple of 9, then n² is at least 9’ (whether or not the original is true for all integers n)?
options: If n is a multiple of 9, then n² is less than 9.
If n² is less than 9, then n is not a multiple of 9.
If n is not a multiple of 9, then n² is at least 9.
If n² is at least 9, then n is a multiple of 9.
If n is not a multiple of 9, then n² is less than 9.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is not-Q ⇒ not-P. Here that reads: if n² is less than 9, then n is not a multiple of 9. The two fail in exactly the same case (P true and Q false). Swapping without negating instead gives the converse.

questions.stem: Which statement follows the contrapositive rule for ‘If n is a multiple of 7, then n² is at least 49’ (whether or not the original is true for all integers n)?
options: If n² is less than 49, then n is not a multiple of 7.
If n is a multiple of 7, then n² is less than 49.
If n is not a multiple of 7, then n² is less than 49.
If n is not a multiple of 7, then n² is at least 49.
If n² is at least 49, then n is a multiple of 7.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is not-Q ⇒ not-P. Here that reads: if n² is less than 49, then n is not a multiple of 7. The two fail in exactly the same case (P true and Q false). Swapping without negating instead gives the converse.

questions.stem: Which statement is true over the reals?
options: There is a real y greater than every real x.
Every real x has a real y greater than it.
Every positive x has a positive y less than both x and 0.
There is a real y less than every real x.
Every real x has a negative real y greater than it.
questions.explanation: Choose y=x+1 for each x. No fixed real can exceed or fall below all reals, and the sign restrictions invalidate the other options.

questions.stem: Which statement is equivalent to a set S containing no negative real?
options: Every x in S is positive.
There is a nonnegative x in S.
There is a real t>0 with S contained in (t,∞).
Every x in S is nonnegative.
There is a negative x outside S.
questions.explanation: Each member must individually avoid being negative. Zero is permitted and the condition also holds for the empty set.

questions.stem: For real numbers 0 < x < 2, which statement about y is true?
options: There is a real y satisfying x < y < 2 for all such x.
There is a real y satisfying 0 < y < x for all such x.
For every such x there is a real y satisfying 0 < y < x.
For every such x there is a real y satisfying 2 < y < x.
Every y in (0, 2) is smaller than every such x.
questions.explanation: The choice y = x/2 works in the third statement. No fixed positive y is smaller than all positive x in (0, 2), and no fixed y below 2 is larger than all x below 2. The other inequalities are not possible as stated.

questions.stem: Which is true for the positive integers?
options: There is an even m such that m>n for every n.
For every n there is an even m such that m>n.
For every even m there is an n such that n<m and n is even.
Every n exceeds some positive n.
There is an odd m such that m²=n for every n.
questions.explanation: Take m=2n+2. There is no universal upper bound, 2 has no smaller positive even integer, and 1 has no smaller positive integer.

questions.stem: Let A={1,2} and B={2,3}. Which assertion is false?
options: Every a in A has a b in B with a≤b.
Some b in B is at least every a in A.
Every b in B has an a in A with a<b.
Some a in A exceeds every b in B.
Some a in A equals some b in B.
questions.explanation: No a is greater than 3. The choices b=3, b=3, a=1 and a=b=2 witness the other four assertions respectively.

questions.stem: For x in (0,1), which correctly expresses that f(x) has no upper bound?
options: For every real M there exists x with f(x)>M.
There is an x with f(x)>M for every real M.
For every x there exists M with f(x)>M.
For some M every x satisfies f(x)<M.
For some M there exists x with f(x)>M.
questions.explanation: An upper bound is a real M with every f(x)≤M. Negating both quantifiers and the inequality gives the stated condition.

questions.stem: Let S = {−2, −1, 1, 2}. Which holds for the equation xy = 1 when x and y are restricted to S?
options: Every x has a suitable y.
There is a fixed y that works for all x.
Some x have a suitable y and some do not.
Every x has two suitable values of y.
No x has a suitable y.
questions.explanation: For x = 1 or −1 the matching y is x itself. For x = ±2 the unique real candidate would be ±1/2, which is outside S.

questions.stem: For x in (1,2), which quantity can be chosen once, independently of x, to make x<y always true?
questions.explanation: The excluded endpoint 2 exceeds every allowed x. The middle formula choices depend on x, while fixed numbers below 2 are exceeded by some x.

questions.stem:
All variables range over the integers from 0 to 10. Which statements hold?
I. For every x there is a y such that x + y leaves remainder 3 on division by 11.
II. Some fixed y works for every x.
III. Every pair (x, y) works.
questions.explanation: I works: take the unique representative y of 3 − x modulo 11 in the required range. II fails because x = 0 and x = 1 require different y. III would imply II, so also fails.

questions.stem:
All variables range over the integers from 0 to 10. Which statements hold?
I. For every x there is a y such that x + y leaves remainder 1 on division by 11.
II. Some fixed y works for every x.
III. Every pair (x, y) works.
questions.explanation: I works: take the unique representative y of 1 − x modulo 11 in the required range. II fails because x = 0 and x = 1 require different y. III would imply II, so also fails.

questions.stem: Which continuous function refutes “if f(−1)=f(1), then f(0)=f(1)”?
questions.explanation: The square has endpoint values 1 and central value 0. The odd cube and linear function fail the premise, and the last two are constant.

questions.stem: Which pair (a,b) disproves “if a<0<b, then the midpoint of [a,b] is positive”?
questions.explanation: Only (−3,1) meets the sign premise and gives a midpoint at or below zero.

questions.stem: A student claims that whenever a real number x satisfies −2 < x < 3, its square satisfies x² < 4. Which of these values disproves the claim?
questions.explanation: The counterexample must be inside the open interval and have square at least 4. The value 2 lies in the interval and gives exactly 4. Both −2 and 3 fail the premise.

questions.stem: Which interval refutes “if x²<4 for every x in I then −1<x<2 for every x in I”?
questions.explanation: Every point in (−2,0) has square below 4, but this interval includes −1. The other intervals either include points of square at least 4 or satisfy the conclusion.

questions.stem: For which polynomial is the claim “if f has a root in (−1,1), then some root lies in (0,1)” false?
questions.explanation: The root 0 meets the premise but fails the strict positive condition, and the other root 2 is outside (0,1).

questions.stem: Which sequence of signs at x=0,1,2, in that order, is sufficient to refute “if f is nonnegative at both endpoints of [0,2], then f is nonnegative throughout”?
questions.explanation: Zero is nonnegative at the left endpoint, but a negative central value violates the conclusion.

questions.stem: A student claims that every real root of x² + bx + c = 0 lies in (0, 1) whenever b < 0 and c > 0. Which pair (b, c) provides a counterexample?
questions.explanation: For (−3, 2) the polynomial factors as (x − 1)(x − 2) and neither root lies in (0, 1). The first two pairs fail the premise. The third gives no real roots and the fourth gives only 1/2.

questions.stem: Which value disproves the claim that every x in [−2,2] with x²<1 has x>0?
questions.explanation: The value −1/2 lies in the interval and squares to 1/4, but it is not positive.

questions.stem: A student claims: for every integer x, if (x − 7)(x − 11) ≤ 0 then x ≥ 11. Which value refutes the claim?
questions.explanation: The premise holds on [7, 11]; the conclusion fails below 11. A counterexample must satisfy both requirements. 9 lies in [7, 10], and none of the other offered integers does.

questions.stem: A student claims: for every integer x, if (x − 3)(x − 15) ≤ 0 then x ≥ 6. Which value refutes the claim?
questions.explanation: The premise holds on [3, 15]; the conclusion fails below 6. A counterexample must satisfy both requirements. 4 lies in [3, 5], and none of the other offered integers does.

questions.stem: Which pair (a,b) refutes “if a²+b²≤16, then |a|+|b|≤4”?
questions.explanation: The pair (3,2) gives square sum 13 and absolute sum 5. The pairs with square sums 17 and 18 violate the premise.

questions.stem: Which integer x refutes “if (x−4)²≤4 then x is strictly between 2 and 6”?
questions.explanation: At 2 the square reaches the allowed bound of 4, but the strict conclusion excludes 2.

questions.stem: Which pair refutes “if a² + b² > 5, then at least one of a and b is greater than 2”?
questions.explanation: The pair (2, −2) gives 8 > 5, yet both coordinates are at most 2. The first, second and fourth pairs fail the strict premise, and the last satisfies the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which point refutes “if x²+y²=25, then at least one coordinate is greater than or equal to 4”?
questions.explanation: The point (−5,0) is on the circle but neither coordinate reaches 4. The last point is not on the circle.

questions.stem: Which number disproves “if x²≥x, then x≥1”?
questions.explanation: A negative x has nonnegative square, so it satisfies the premise while being below 1.

questions.stem: Which pair (a,b) disproves “if (a−b)²<4, then |a|+|b|<4”?
questions.explanation: At (3,3) the difference is zero while the absolute values sum to 6. The two latter choices fail the strict premise.

questions.stem: Which value disproves the claim that x² > 2x whenever x is nonzero?
questions.explanation: The premise excludes zero, even though the inequality fails there. At x = 1/2, the square is 1/4 and 2x is 1, so the inequality fails for a permitted x.

questions.stem: Which inequality is guaranteed whenever x²+y²<2?
questions.explanation: Since (x−y)²≥0, (x+y)²≤2(x²+y²)<4, so x+y<2. A single coordinate can exceed 1, absolute values can sum to more than 1, and opposite signs are possible.

questions.stem: Which offered integer x disproves ‘if (3x + 3)² < 1089, then |x| < 10’?
questions.explanation: To disprove the implication use |x| ≥ 10 and make the square strictly less than 1089. At x = −10, the squared base has magnitude |3 − 30|, strictly less than 33 since both 3 and 30 are positive. At 10 the bound is met exactly, and larger positive x also fails the premise; the remaining choices satisfy the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which offered integer x disproves ‘if (5x + 5)² < 225, then |x| < 2’?
questions.explanation: To disprove the implication use |x| ≥ 2 and make the square strictly less than 225. At x = −2, the squared base has magnitude |5 − 10|, strictly less than 15 since both 5 and 10 are positive. At 2 the bound is met exactly, and larger positive x also fails the premise; the remaining choices satisfy the conclusion.

questions.stem: Someone solves x(x−2)=3x by cancelling x to get x=5. Which description is correct?
questions.explanation: Moving all terms to one side gives x(x−5)=0. Cancelling x omits the case x=0.

questions.stem: After dividing (x+1)(x²−4)=0 by x+1, which root of the original equation has been omitted?
questions.explanation: The divided equation retains roots ±2. The root of x+1 is distinct from them.

questions.stem: A proof that the equation 2x³ = 8x has exactly two real solutions begins “divide by x to obtain 2x² = 8”. What additional case must be checked to know the exact number of solutions?
questions.explanation: The division is valid for every nonzero x and gives ±2. It omits precisely x = 0, which also solves the original equation. In total there are three distinct solutions.

questions.stem: In solving (x−3)²=5(x−3), a student wants to divide by x−3. Which condition is sufficient to make the division valid?
questions.explanation: The divisor vanishes only at 3. Even x excludes 3, while every other condition allows it.

questions.stem: A student divides sin x cos x=sin x by sin x while working on [0,π]. How many original solutions does the divided equation miss?
questions.explanation: The original allows x=0 or π where sin x=0. The resulting equation cos x=1 keeps 0 but misses π.

questions.stem: In a proof that two expressions are equal, the author shows (a−b)(U−V)=0. Which extra assertion suffices to conclude U=V?
questions.explanation: If a−b is nonzero then the product can vanish only through U−V. None of the other assertions rules out a=b=1.

questions.stem: For which real x does x/(x² + x) = 1/(x + 1) hold with both sides defined?
questions.explanation: Factor the left denominator as x(x + 1). Both 0 and −1 are excluded before cancellation. At every other value cancellation gives the right side.

questions.stem: For which equation does cancelling a common factor x from both sides yield an equation with the same real solutions?
questions.explanation: The reduced last equation is x+1=1, which still yields the root x=0. Each other reduced equation is false at zero.

questions.stem:
A student tries to solve (x − 6)(x − 5) = 0 over the reals.
1. Divide both sides by x − 6, getting x − 5 = 0.
2. Add 5 to both sides, getting x = 5.
3. Substitute x = 5 into the starting equation to check it.
4. Report that x = 5 is the only solution.
Where is the first invalid deduction?
options: Step 3: substitution is not allowed after factoring
Step 4: the preceding steps are all equivalences
Step 2: adding a number can change an equality
Step 1: it can discard a zero-factor case
questions.explanation: Step 1 restricts to x ≠ 6, without examining x = 6. At that discarded value the original product is zero. Alternatively, a product of two real numbers is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero, yielding 6 and 5.

questions.stem:
A student tries to solve (x − 9)(x − 12) = 0 over the reals.
1. Divide both sides by x − 9, getting x − 12 = 0.
2. Add 12 to both sides, getting x = 12.
3. Substitute x = 12 into the starting equation to check it.
4. Report that x = 12 is the only solution.
Where is the first invalid deduction?
options: Step 2: adding a number can change an equality
Step 3: substitution is not allowed after factoring
Step 4: the preceding steps are all equivalences
Step 1: it can discard a zero-factor case
questions.explanation: Step 1 restricts to x ≠ 9, without examining x = 9. At that discarded value the original product is zero. Alternatively, a product of two real numbers is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero, yielding 9 and 12.

questions.stem: A solution to √(x+6)=x squares both sides and obtains x=−2 or 3. Which solutions are valid?
questions.explanation: The square root is nonnegative, so x=−2 is extraneous, and x=3 checks in the original equation.

questions.stem: The equation |2x−1|=3 has roots p<q. A student considers just 2x−1=3. What value of p is missed?
questions.explanation: The omitted branch is 2x−1=−3, which gives x=−1.

questions.stem: For a real number a, a student concludes from a² ≥ 9 that a ≥ 3. Which statement correctly repairs the conclusion without any extra assumption?
questions.explanation: Taking the nonnegative square root yields |a| ≥ 3, so a lies at least 3 units from zero in either direction. Both endpoints are included.

questions.stem: If x is real, which expression always equals √((x−4)²)?
questions.explanation: The square root of a square is the magnitude of its base, never a negative number.

questions.stem: Which x disproves “if x²>9, then x>3”?
questions.explanation: Its square exceeds 9 but it is on the negative side of the root boundary.

questions.stem: For x<0, which inequality is equivalent to x²<25?
questions.explanation: The full inequality is −5<x<5. Its restriction to x<0 has lower boundary −5, excluded.

questions.stem: Let a and b be real with a² = b² and a + b > 0. Which conclusion follows?
options: a and b are both negative
Exactly one of a and b is zero
a = b and both are positive
a and b have opposite signs
questions.explanation: The factorisation (a − b)(a + b) = 0 gives one of two cases. The strictly positive sum rules out a + b = 0, so a = b. Their positive sum then requires a = b > 0.

questions.stem: An argument uses a²=b² to infer a=b. Which added assumption always makes the inference valid?
questions.explanation: Equal squares give a=b or a=−b. In the latter case ab=−b² can be nonnegative only when both vanish.

questions.stem:
A proof claims that (x − 3)² = 100 implies x = 13.
1. Take nonnegative square roots of both sides.
2. Replace √((x − 3)²) with x − 3.
3. Simplify the right side to 10.
4. Solve x − 3 = 10.
Which is the first unjustified step?
options: Step 4: adding the same constant does not preserve equality
Step 1: square roots cannot be taken on both sides of this equality
Step 2: the square root is an absolute value
Step 3: the nonnegative square root is negative
questions.explanation: The expressions on both sides are nonnegative, so step 1 is allowed. But √(u²) = |u|, not necessarily u. Solving |x − 3| = 10 yields 13 and -7; the second value is lost in step 2.

questions.stem:
A proof claims that (x − 3)² = 196 implies x = 17.
1. Take nonnegative square roots of both sides.
2. Replace √((x − 3)²) with x − 3.
3. Simplify the right side to 14.
4. Solve x − 3 = 14.
Which is the first unjustified step?
options: Step 4: adding the same constant does not preserve equality
Step 3: the nonnegative square root is negative
Step 2: the square root is an absolute value
Step 1: square roots cannot be taken on both sides of this equality
questions.explanation: The expressions on both sides are nonnegative, so step 1 is allowed. But √(u²) = |u|, not necessarily u. Solving |x − 3| = 14 yields 17 and -11; the second value is lost in step 2.

questions.stem: For x<0, which inequality is equivalent to x²<−3x?
questions.explanation: Divide by the negative x, reversing the comparison to x>−3.

questions.stem: If a<b<0, which chain is correct?
questions.explanation: Both reciprocals are negative. Multiplying a<b by positive 1/(ab) gives 1/b<1/a.

questions.stem: To study 1/(x − 1) > 1 for x ≠ 1, a student multiplies by x − 1 and concludes x < 2. Which is the correct solution set?
questions.explanation: If x < 1, the reciprocal is negative and cannot exceed 1. If x > 1, multiplying by the positive denominator gives 1 > x − 1, so precisely 1 < x < 2 works.

questions.stem: Which condition makes “a<b implies ab<a²” true for all b>a?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a² gives a(b−a). Since the second factor is positive, the product is strictly negative exactly when a<0.

questions.stem: Given 0<a<b, which quantity must be least?
questions.explanation: The quantity −b is below both −a and a−b, and is negative. The last two quantities are nonnegative.

questions.stem: For −4<x<−1, what is the range of 2−3x?
questions.explanation: The transformation is decreasing. The endpoints −4 and −1 give 14 and 5, neither attained.

questions.stem: A proof says that if x² + 1 = 5, then x² = 4, then x > 0, and finally x = 2. Which implication could replace the third step so that solving the equation produces all its real solutions?
questions.explanation: The equation x² = 4 factors to (x − 2)(x + 2) = 0. Both roots solve the starting equation. Restricting to positive x is the unsupported step.

questions.stem: For real x≠0, when does 1/x>1 hold?
questions.explanation: Negative x gives a negative reciprocal. Positive x permits multiplication without reversing the inequality and yields x<1.

questions.stem: A proof starts from −3(x + 4) < −30. It divides both sides by −3 and writes x + 4 < 10, then gives x < 6. What must be changed to give an equivalent bound?
options: The final bound should be x > 6.
The final bound should be x < 14.
Division must be replaced by subtraction of the coefficient.
The final bound should be x ≥ 6.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a negative reverses the inequality: x + 4 > 10. Subtract 4 without reversing to obtain x > 6. At equality the starting inequality is false; replacing > with ≥ adds a spurious solution.

questions.stem: A proof starts from −8(x + 7) < −96. It divides both sides by −8 and writes x + 7 < 12, then gives x < 5. What must be changed to give an equivalent bound?
options: Division must be replaced by subtraction of the coefficient.
The final bound should be x ≥ 5.
The final bound should be x < 19.
The final bound should be x > 5.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a negative reverses the inequality: x + 7 > 12. Subtract 7 without reversing to obtain x > 5. At equality the starting inequality is false; replacing > with ≥ adds a spurious solution.

questions.stem: Assume that if n is a multiple of 6 then P holds, and if P holds then n is even. Which conclusion follows?
options: If n is even then P holds.
If P fails then 6 does not divide n.
If n is odd then 6 divides n.
If 6 does not divide n then P fails.
P holds exactly for even n.
questions.explanation: A multiple of 6 would force P, so failure of P rules it out. Even integers not divisible by 6 are not constrained further.

questions.stem: For x in a set S, x>2 forces f(x)>1, and f(x)>1 forces g(x)≤0. If g(x)>0, what must hold?
questions.explanation: The positive g rules out f(x)>1, which in turn rules out x>2. No premise rules out equality at 2.

questions.stem: Statements A, B and C obey these two rules: if A is true then B is true, and if C is true then B is false. Which conclusion is forced?
options: A and C are both true.
A and C cannot both be false.
A and C cannot both be true.
C being false forces A to be true.
B being true forces A to be true.
questions.explanation: If A and C were both true, B would have to be both true and false. When A and C are false the two rules impose no further condition, so the remaining proposed deductions need not hold.

questions.stem: If P holds, Q holds. If Q holds, R is false. If R is false, P is false. Which must hold?
questions.explanation: Starting with P leads to its own negation. With P false, Q can be either truth value, and R is not forced true.

questions.stem: Sets A,B,C satisfy A⊆B and B∩C=∅. What follows?
questions.explanation: Any member of A is in B, which has no member in common with C. For example disjoint nonempty A and C with B strictly containing A show the other conclusions are not forced.

questions.stem: If a statement S implies T and S implies U, which conclusion always follows?
options: If not T or not U then not S.
If both T and U then S.
If not S then neither T nor U.
questions.explanation: Either failed consequence is enough to rule out S. Neither implication can be reversed without another premise.

questions.stem: A positive integer n satisfies: if 5 divides n, then 3 divides n; if 3 does not divide n, then 2 divides n. Which condition can be deduced from these two implications?
options: If n is even, it is not divisible by 5.
If n is odd, it is divisible by 5.
If n is odd, it is divisible by 3.
If 5 does not divide n, then 3 does not divide n.
If 3 divides n, then n is odd.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of the second implication gives odd implies divisible by 3. The other conclusions fail for n = 30, 3, 3 and 6 respectively; these satisfy both given rules.

questions.stem: Suppose V is true exactly when W is false, and W being true implies X being true. Which conclusion is forced?
options: If X is false, V is true.
If V is true, X is false.
If X is true, W is true.
If W is false, X is false.
If V is true, W is true.
questions.explanation: A false X forces a false W, which is equivalent to a true V. X may be true even with false W.

questions.stem: Four assertions P, Q, R and S have unknown truth values. Three facts are established: if Q fails, then R holds; if R holds, then S fails; and if P holds, then S fails. Which conclusion follows from these facts alone?
options: If Q fails, then P holds.
If R fails, then S holds.
If S holds, then Q holds.
If S fails, then R holds.
If P holds, then Q fails.
questions.explanation: Combine the first two implications: if Q fails, then S fails. Its contrapositive is: if S holds, then Q holds. The third fact points to the same conclusion as the second and does not reverse either implication.

questions.stem: Four assertions P, Q, R and S have unknown truth values. Three facts are established: if R holds, then S fails; if S fails, then P holds; and if Q fails, then P holds. Which conclusion follows from these facts alone?
options: If Q fails, then R holds.
If P holds, then S fails.
If S holds, then P fails.
If P fails, then R fails.
If R holds, then Q fails.
questions.explanation: Combine the first two implications: if R holds, then P holds. Its contrapositive is: if P fails, then R fails. The third fact points to the same conclusion as the second and does not reverse either implication.

questions.stem: A five-entry string uses just A and B. Which condition guarantees two adjacent entries are both A?
options: At least two entries are A.
At least three entries are A.
At least four entries are A.
There is a B at the end.
There are more As than Bs.
questions.explanation: Without adjacent As, at most three fit (in positions 1,3,5). The string ABABA shows three are not enough.

questions.stem: Among eight consecutive integers, how many must be divisible by 4?
questions.explanation: Partition the block into two sets of four consecutive integers. Each meets every residue modulo 4 once.

questions.stem: Mark the multiples of 5 and the integers that are one more than a multiple of 5. What is the shortest length of a block of consecutive integers that guarantees two marks in the block?
questions.explanation: Any five consecutive integers contain each residue modulo 5 once, giving two marks. The block 1, 2, 3, 4 has only one mark, so four cannot guarantee two.

questions.stem: The selected positions in {1,…,10} have no consecutive pair. What is the maximum possible number selected?
questions.explanation: Each pair (1,2), (3,4), …, (9,10) contributes at most one. All odd positions reach five.

questions.stem: Six points are placed on a line at distinct integer positions from 0 to 12. What is the greatest possible value of the shortest gap between consecutive points?
questions.explanation: The five gaps total at most 12, so the shortest is at most 2 as an integer. Positions 0,2,4,6,8,10 attain this.

questions.stem: How many consecutive nonmultiples of 6 can occur at most?
questions.explanation: Every block of six contains a multiple of 6; the five numbers 1 through 5 show this bound is sharp.

questions.stem: A row of 11 squares contains exactly three black squares. What is the minimum possible length of its longest run of consecutive nonblack squares?
questions.explanation: The black squares split the eight others into four runs, allowing empty runs. At least one run has length ≥ 2 because four runs of length at most 1 hold at most four squares. Place black squares at positions 3, 6 and 9 to make all four runs of length 2.

questions.stem: Ten entries in a row contain three marked positions. What is the least possible length of the longest run of unmarked positions?
questions.explanation: There are seven unmarked positions in at most four gaps. One gap must have two or more, and gap lengths 2,2,2,1 attain two.

questions.stem: For an integer t, call t marked if one of t + 3, t + 5, t + 2 is divisible by 8. What is the least length of a block of consecutive integers guaranteed to contain a marked integer?
questions.explanation:
Mark the residues 3, 5, 6 on a cycle of length 8. Successive marks have gaps 2, 1, 5 (include the wrap-around). A gap of g contains g − 1 unmarked integers. The longest block that can avoid a mark therefore has length 4; add one.

Answer: 5.

questions.stem: For an integer t, call t marked if one of t + 2, t + 0, t + 1 is divisible by 5. What is the least length of a block of consecutive integers guaranteed to contain a marked integer?
questions.explanation:
Mark the residues 0, 3, 4 on a cycle of length 5. Successive marks have gaps 3, 1, 1 (include the wrap-around). A gap of g contains g − 1 unmarked integers. The longest block that can avoid a mark therefore has length 2; add one.

Answer: 3.

questions.stem: The positive integers a,b are coprime and ab=36. How many ordered pairs (a,b) are possible?
questions.explanation: Each full prime power 4 and 9 goes to just one factor. The two independent choices give four assignments.

questions.stem: If positive coprime a,b have 18 dividing ab and 3 dividing a, what must divide a?
questions.explanation: No factor of 3 can occur in b. Both copies of 3 required by 18 must be in a. The pair (9,2) rules out the other options.

questions.stem: Positive integers a and b have no common factor greater than 1. If a²b³ is a perfect sixth power, which must be true?
options: a is a perfect square and b is a perfect cube.
a is a perfect cube and b is a perfect square.
Both a and b are multiples of 6.
a is a sixth power, with no restriction on b.
questions.explanation: No prime occurs in both factors. For a prime of exponent e in a, 2e is a multiple of 6, so e is a multiple of 3. For one of exponent e in b, 3e is a multiple of 6, so e is even. For example a = 8, b = 9 shows the conclusion is no stronger than cube and square respectively.

questions.stem: If a,b are coprime positive integers and a divides b², what must a equal?
questions.explanation: Every prime dividing b² divides b. Any prime factor of a would therefore contradict coprimality.

questions.stem: For coprime positive a,b, what is gcd(a+b,ab)?
questions.explanation: A prime dividing ab must divide a or b. If it also divided a+b, it would divide both, contradicting coprimality.

questions.stem: Which pair refutes the assertion “if ab is a perfect cube, then both factors are perfect cubes”?
questions.explanation: Here ab=8 but 2 and 4 are not cubes. The other choices either do not have a cube product or have cube factors.

questions.stem: Positive integers a and b are coprime and ab = 72. What is the smallest possible value of a + b?
questions.explanation: The prime powers 8 and 9 must each stay together in one factor. Up to swapping, the only pairs are (1, 72) and (8, 9), so the minimum sum is 17.

questions.stem: A reduced fraction a/b is squared and its result is 16/81. If a,b are positive, what is a+b?
questions.explanation: Since coprime a,b have coprime squares, the displayed reduced numerator and denominator must be 16 and 81, giving a=4 and b=9.

questions.stem: For N = 2^4 × 7^4, how many ordered pairs (u, v) of positive integers satisfy uv = N and have no common factor greater than 1?
questions.explanation:
If a prime occurs in both factors they share that divisor. Thus each of the blocks 2^4 and 7^4 must go wholly to one of u and v, with two independent choices. All assignments work (including those with a factor 1).

Answer: 4.

questions.stem: For N = 2^2 × 11^4, how many ordered pairs (u, v) of positive integers satisfy uv = N and have no common factor greater than 1?
questions.explanation:
If a prime occurs in both factors they share that divisor. Thus each of the blocks 2^2 and 11^4 must go wholly to one of u and v, with two independent choices. All assignments work (including those with a factor 1).

Answer: 4.

questions.stem: Which integer expression is always odd?
questions.explanation: One of n and n+1 is even, so their product plus 1 is odd. At n=0 the other expressions are all even.

questions.stem: For integer n, when is n²−1 divisible by 4?
questions.explanation: The squares modulo 4 are 1 for odd n and 0 for even n.

questions.stem: If a and b are integers and a² − b² is odd, which statement must hold?
options: Both a and b are odd.
Both a and b are even.
a and b have the same parity.
Exactly one of a and b is even.
The parity of a + b can be either even or odd.
questions.explanation: Squaring preserves parity. A difference of two squares is odd only when one square is even and one is odd, so the original integers have opposite parity.

questions.stem: For which parity pattern is a+b+ab even?
options: One even and one odd only.
questions.explanation: Since a+b+ab=(a+1)(b+1)−1, it is even exactly when both shifted factors are odd.

questions.stem: How many integers n from 0 through 15 make n(n−1)/2 odd?
questions.explanation: The product is 2 modulo 4 for n≡2 or 3 modulo 4. Each residue occurs four times.

questions.stem: The squares of two integers have an odd sum. Which must also be odd?
questions.explanation: Squares preserve parity, so the integers have opposite parity. Their difference is then odd.

questions.stem: For which integers n is (n + 1)(n + 3) odd?
questions.explanation: The two factors have the same parity, both opposite to n. The product is odd exactly when both factors are odd, so precisely when n is even.

questions.stem: Which statement holds for every odd integer n?
questions.explanation: The even neighbours n−1 and n+1 differ by 2; one is divisible by 4 and the other by 2. The example n=3 rules out 16.

questions.stem: What can be concluded about the parity of n² + 7n + 1 over all integers n?
options: It is odd for every integer n.
It is even exactly when n is even.
It is even exactly when n is odd.
Its parity changes between some integers of the same parity.
It is even for every integer n.
questions.explanation: Modulo 2, n² has the same remainder as n, so the expression has remainder (8)n + 1 modulo 2. For even n it is 1; for odd n it is 1. Remainder 0 means even; remainder 1 means odd.

questions.stem: What can be concluded about the parity of n² + 3n + 8 over all integers n?
options: It is odd for every integer n.
It is even for every integer n.
Its parity changes between some integers of the same parity.
It is even exactly when n is odd.
It is even exactly when n is even.
questions.explanation: Modulo 2, n² has the same remainder as n, so the expression has remainder (4)n + 8 modulo 2. For even n it is 0; for odd n it is 0. Remainder 0 means even; remainder 1 means odd.

questions.stem: What is the smallest number of distinct integers from {1,…,8} that guarantees two selected integers sum to 9?
questions.explanation: Partition into four pairs with sum 9. Choosing five forces a complete pair, while choosing 1,2,3,4 does not.

questions.stem: If seven objects are placed in three boxes, how many in a single box are guaranteed?
questions.explanation: At most two per box would allow only six. Counts 3,2,2 show that three is sharp.

questions.stem: Six boxes are labelled 1 through 6. Two boxes form a matching pair when their labels sum to 7. How many boxes must be selected to guarantee a matching pair even after one of the selected boxes is removed?
questions.explanation: With five boxes selected, two of the three matching pairs are complete. Removing one box can break only one pair. Four boxes need not suffice: take one pair and one box from each other pair, then remove a member of the only complete pair.

questions.stem: Five distinct integers are chosen from {0,…,9}. Which statement is forced?
questions.explanation: Five objects in two parity classes force a match. The selection {0,2,4,6,8} avoids adjacency and a sum of 9; {1,2,3,4,5} avoids both endpoints.

questions.stem: How many integers must be chosen to guarantee two have a difference divisible by 7?
questions.explanation: There are seven possible remainders. Eight force repetition; 0 through 6 do not.

questions.stem: What is the smallest size of a group that guarantees two people among it were born on the same day of the week?
questions.explanation: At most seven people can all have different weekdays of birth, and seven can do so.

questions.stem: How many integers must be selected from {1, 2, …, 11} to guarantee that two have a difference divisible by 5?
questions.explanation: A difference is divisible by 5 exactly when its endpoints are in the same residue class. There are five classes, so six choices force a repeated class. Choosing 1 through 5 shows five may fail.

questions.stem: Which property is forced in every list of three real numbers selected from [0,6]?
questions.explanation: After sorting, the two consecutive gaps have sum at most 6. They cannot both exceed 3. Three distinct nearby nonintegers rule out the other options.

questions.stem: Take the integers 1 to 16, except 2 and 15. What is the minimum number of distinct remaining integers one must select to guarantee two sum to 17?
questions.explanation:
The integers come in complementary pairs {x, 17 − x}. Exactly one pair has been removed, leaving 7 pairs. Taking one from each shows 7 are not enough; taking one more forces two from a pair.

Answer: 8.

questions.stem: Take the integers 1 to 26, except 7 and 20. What is the minimum number of distinct remaining integers one must select to guarantee two sum to 27?
questions.explanation:
The integers come in complementary pairs {x, 27 − x}. Exactly one pair has been removed, leaving 12 pairs. Taking one from each shows 12 are not enough; taking one more forces two from a pair.

Answer: 13.

questions.stem: A set A has 7 elements and a set B has 5 elements. Their union has 9 elements. How many are in exactly one of the sets?
questions.explanation: The intersection has 7+5−9=3 members. Remove them from the union to count the six others.

questions.stem: Two subsets of a 12-element set each have size 8. What is the smallest possible intersection?
questions.explanation: Their union has size at most 12, requiring overlap at least 16−12. Two subsets sharing four and each using four different remaining elements attain it.

questions.stem: In a group of ten people, six play tennis and six play chess. Exactly one person plays neither. How many play both?
questions.explanation: Nine people play at least one. Adding the two counts gives twelve, counting each person in both groups twice. The excess above nine is three.

questions.stem: Sets A and B are disjoint of sizes 3 and 4. A third set C has exactly two members in each of A and B. What is the smallest possible size of C?
questions.explanation: The two members in A are different from the two in B, and no other members of C are required.

questions.stem: In a class of 20, 14 pupils study X, 12 study Y, and everyone studies at least one. How many study only Y?
questions.explanation: Everyone outside X must be in Y. There are 20−14 such pupils.

questions.stem: What is the greatest possible size of A∩B∩C if the pairwise intersections A∩B, B∩C and C∩A have sizes 3,4 and 5 respectively?
questions.explanation: The triple intersection is contained in the smallest pair intersection. A shared core of three, with one extra element shared only by B,C and two shared only by C,A, attains it.

questions.stem: Two sets A and B each have six elements and are contained in a universe of ten elements. Which size of A ∪ B is impossible?
questions.explanation: The union must contain all six members of A, so it cannot have size five. The other sizes are possible by letting B share six, five, four or three elements respectively with A.

questions.stem: A set S has eight elements. Subsets A and B both contain the same fixed element of S and have sizes 3 and 5. How many elements of S must lie outside A∪B at a minimum?
questions.explanation: The overlap is at least one, so the union has at most seven. Taking the remaining two and four members disjoint attains seven.

questions.stem: S and T are subsets of a set of size 34, with sizes 29 and 33. What is the difference between the largest and smallest possible values of |S ∩ T|?
questions.explanation:
The intersection is at most min(29, 33) = 29, attained by nesting. It is at least max(0, 29 + 33 − 34) = 28, from the union bound; placing as many elements as possible outside the other set attains this. Subtract the endpoints.

Answer: 1.

questions.stem: S and T are subsets of a set of size 19, with sizes 9 and 17. What is the difference between the largest and smallest possible values of |S ∩ T|?
questions.explanation:
The intersection is at most min(9, 17) = 9, attained by nesting. It is at least max(0, 9 + 17 − 19) = 7, from the union bound; placing as many elements as possible outside the other set attains this. Subtract the endpoints.

Answer: 2.

questions.stem: Which is never the last digit of a perfect square?
questions.explanation: The square's last digit depends only on its root's last digit. The distinct residues obtained are 0,1,4,5,6,9.

questions.stem: How many distinct remainders can n³ leave on division by 7?
questions.explanation: Cubing residues 0 through 6 gives 0,1,1,6,1,6,6. There are three distinct results.

questions.stem: For an integer n, which remainder cannot occur when n² + 1 is divided by 8?
questions.explanation: Squares modulo 8 are 0, 1 and 4: odd squares give 1 and even squares give 0 or 4. Adding 1 gives 1, 2 and 5, so 4 cannot occur.

questions.stem: What is the remainder of a²+b² on division by 4 if a and b are both odd?
options: It depends on a and b
questions.explanation: Each odd square is 1 modulo 4, so their sum is 2 modulo 4.

questions.stem: What is the remainder when 3²⁰ is divided by 7?
questions.explanation: Since 3³≡−1 modulo 7, 3⁶≡1. Reduce the exponent 20 to 2, giving 9≡2.

questions.stem: For how many residues r modulo 8 does r²≡r modulo 8?
questions.explanation: The product r(r−1) must be divisible by 8. Exactly one factor is even, so that factor must be divisible by 8, giving r=0 or 1.

questions.stem: Which list gives all possible remainders when 2n² + 3n is divided by 6, for integer n?
questions.explanation: The expression depends only on the remainder of n modulo 6. Substituting 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 gives remainders 0, 5, 2, 3, 2 and 5 respectively. Taking the distinct results gives the final list.

questions.stem: Which list gives all possible remainders of n²−n+1 on division by 5?
questions.explanation: Testing n≡0,1,2,3,4 gives 1,1,3,2,3. The distinct values are 1,2,3.

questions.stem: Which list gives exactly the remainders of integers n for which 5 divides n(n + 1)?
questions.explanation: Write n = 5k + s. Expanding shows n(n + 1) has the same remainder as s(s + 1). For s = 0 through 4, the respective remainders are 0, 2, 1, 2, 0. Keep exactly the positions where the remainder is zero.

questions.stem: Which list gives exactly the remainders of integers n for which 11 divides n(n + 4)?
questions.explanation: Write n = 11k + s. Expanding shows n(n + 4) has the same remainder as s(s + 4). For s = 0 through 10, the respective remainders are 0, 5, 1, 10, 10, 1, 5, 0, 8, 7, 8. Keep exactly the positions where the remainder is zero.

questions.stem: A positive sequence starts at 3 and every step replaces a term t by 12/t. What is its 20th term?
questions.explanation: Two steps return to the same term. The even indices have the second term 12/3=4.

questions.stem: An ordered pair (a,b) is replaced by (a−2,b+2) each step. Starting at (9,1), which pair cannot occur?
questions.explanation: Each coordinate retains its parity. The four pairs with odd coordinates occur in the first four steps.

questions.stem: A move transfers two counters from one pile to the other. The two piles start with 5 and 9 counters. Which unordered pair of pile sizes is impossible to obtain?
questions.explanation: Each pile keeps its original parity because its size changes by 2. The only listed pair with even sizes is 4 and 10. The other pairs occur by transferring counters from one pile to the other the required number of times.

questions.stem: A sequence starts with a₁=1 and a₂=2 and satisfies aₙ₊₂=aₙ₊₁−aₙ. What is a₂₀?
questions.explanation: The first six terms are 1,2,1,−1,−2,−1. Then the pair 1,2 repeats, so index 20 is equivalent to index 2.

questions.stem: Starting at 1, a number may be repeatedly increased by 4 or decreased by 6. Which value is impossible to reach?
questions.explanation: Each move is even, so the number stays odd. The other targets are reachable by one −6, one of each move, two +4 followed by one −6, and one +4 respectively.

questions.stem: Each move on a pair (a,b) replaces it by (b,a+b). Starting with two odd integers, which describes when the first coordinate is even?
questions.explanation: The parity pairs cycle (odd,odd), (odd,even), (even,odd), then back. The first coordinate is even at move number 2 modulo 3.

questions.stem: Start with the pair (1, 6). At every step, either increase the first entry by 2 and decrease the second by 1, or decrease the first by 2 and increase the second by 1. Which pair is impossible to reach?
questions.explanation: The first entry plus twice the second stays equal to 13. The pair (5, 5) would give 15. Repeating the first move from one to four times gives the other four options.

questions.stem: A list starts with six positive entries and no zeros. In one move the signs of exactly two entries are flipped. Which number of negative entries is unreachable?
questions.explanation: Each move changes the number of negatives by −2,0 or 2. All even possibilities are attained by flipping disjoint pairs.

questions.stem: Let u₀ = 4 and uₙ₊₁ = 9uₙ + 11 for every n ≥ 0. What is the remainder of u_6 on division by 8?
questions.explanation:
Since 9 is congruent to 1 modulo 8, each step adds 11 to the residue. Starting from 4 and taking 6 steps gives the same residue as 70. Large terms need not be computed.

Answer: 6.

questions.stem: Let u₀ = 5 and uₙ₊₁ = 12uₙ + 4 for every n ≥ 0. What is the remainder of u_7 on division by 11?
questions.explanation:
Since 12 is congruent to 1 modulo 11, each step adds 4 to the residue. Starting from 5 and taking 7 steps gives the same residue as 33. Large terms need not be computed.

Answer: 0.

questions.stem: An integer set contains 5 and is closed under adding 3. Which number must be in it?
questions.explanation: Applying the rule twice gives 5+3+3=11. The set {5,8,11,…} shows the other values are not forced.

questions.stem: A real set contains 2, and whenever it contains x it contains x². Which membership is not forced?
questions.explanation: Iterated squaring gives 2,4,16,256,…; the set consisting of only these iterates is closed and excludes 8.

questions.stem: A set contains 3 and is closed under the rule “if n belongs, then 2n − 1 belongs”. What is the least possible size of its intersection with {1, 2, …, 20}?
questions.explanation: Starting from 3 the rule forces 5, 9, 17 and 33. These values grow, so after 33 none can return to the target interval. The set consisting of just this sequence satisfies the rule; exactly four of its elements are at most 20.

questions.stem: A subset of the positive integers contains 12. Whenever an even n belongs to it, so does n/2. Which number must belong to it?
questions.explanation: Halving successively gives 6 and then 3. The set {12,6,3} is already closed under the rule.

questions.stem: A collection of real numbers contains 4 and 10, and contains the mean of every pair it contains. Which number must it contain?
questions.explanation: The first mean is 7. Iterating the rule can only produce 4+6k/2^j in [4,10], so cannot produce 6, which requires k/2^j=1/3.

questions.stem: An integer set contains 3 and is closed under negation and adding 4. Which number must it contain?
questions.explanation: Negating 3 and adding 4 twice gives 5. The odd integers form a closed set excluding all other choices.

questions.stem: A set of real numbers contains 1 and 3 and also contains the average of any two of its elements. Which of these numbers must belong?
questions.explanation: Averaging 1 and 3 gives 2, and then averaging 2 and 3 gives 5/2. The set of all numbers in [1, 3] whose reduced denominator is a power of 2 is closed under averaging and excludes the other choices.

questions.stem: A set contains 1. If it contains n, it contains both 2n and 2n+1. Which best describes the positive numbers forced to belong?
questions.explanation: Every integer greater than 1 is twice a smaller positive integer or one more than twice it. Induction gives them all.

questions.stem: A property P of integers is known to hold at 8. Whenever P holds at n it also holds at n + 6. No other information is given. At which offered integer is P forced to hold?
questions.explanation: Starting at 8, repeatedly add 6, so P holds at 8 + 10×6 = 68. A property true exactly at 8, 14, 20, … satisfies the premise and is false at all other offered integers. In particular, forward closure does not allow a step backwards.

questions.stem: A property P of integers is known to hold at 11. Whenever P holds at n it also holds at n + 3. No other information is given. At which offered integer is P forced to hold?
questions.explanation: Starting at 11, repeatedly add 3, so P holds at 11 + 10×3 = 41. A property true exactly at 11, 14, 17, … satisfies the premise and is false at all other offered integers. In particular, forward closure does not allow a step backwards.

questions.stem: If r is a nonzero rational and t is irrational, which expression must be irrational?
questions.explanation: If rt were rational, dividing by nonzero rational r would make t rational. The square-based options can be rational for t=√2, and t+1/t can be rational for t=(3+√5)/2 with r=1.

questions.stem: Which pair of irrational numbers has a rational sum but irrational product?
questions.explanation: The sum of 2+√2 and −√2 is 2 but their product is −2√2−2. The first two products are rational, and the final two sums are irrational.

questions.stem: Which statement about the product of two irrational real numbers is true?
options: It is rational only if the two numbers are equal.
It is irrational only if the two numbers have opposite signs.
It can be rational or irrational even when both numbers are positive.
questions.explanation: The product √2·√2 = 2 is rational, whereas √2·√3 = √6 is irrational. Distinct positive irrational factors may also give a rational product, as √2·√8 = 4.

questions.stem: If t² is rational and t is irrational, which expression must be rational?
questions.explanation: Squaring rational t² gives rational t⁴. The others would make t rational by subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero t², or reciprocation.

questions.stem: Which example disproves “the product of two irrational numbers is irrational,” using two distinct positive factors?
questions.explanation: The factors √2 and √8=2√2 are distinct positive irrationals, but their product is 4.

questions.stem: Let x and y be irrational with x+y rational. What must be true about x−y?
questions.explanation: If x−y were rational, adding it to the rational sum would make 2x rational and then x rational.

questions.stem: Let x be irrational. Suppose xy = 6 for a real number y. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: If y were rational, then x = 6/y would be rational because y ≠ 0. Taking x = √6 gives y = √6, disproving the other proposed requirements on the squares and the sum.

questions.stem: For rational k, when does kt stay irrational for every irrational t?
options: Exactly when k is a nonzero integer.
questions.explanation: Dividing a rational kt by nonzero rational k would make t rational. At k=0 the product is rational, so the only exclusion is zero.

questions.stem: Let x = √91. Which of the following irrational numbers y makes xy rational?
questions.explanation: Multiplying gives c√(91n) for y = c√n. In a perfect square each prime has even exponent. The two primes 13 and 7 occur once in 91; of the offered radicands only 91 contributes a second copy of both without introducing another odd exponent. The resulting product is 455.

questions.stem: Let x = √77. Which of the following irrational numbers y makes xy rational?
questions.explanation: Multiplying gives c√(77n) for y = c√n. In a perfect square each prime has even exponent. The two primes 7 and 11 occur once in 77; of the offered radicands only 77 contributes a second copy of both without introducing another odd exponent. The resulting product is 385.

questions.stem: Which n disproves “every prime p has p+2 prime” when substituted for p?
questions.explanation: The value 2 is prime but 2+2=4 is not. The four other offered primes have p+2 prime.

questions.stem: Which example refutes “every positive integer that is a sum of two squares is itself a square”?
questions.explanation: The positive integer 5 has the required representation but falls strictly between squares 4 and 9.

questions.stem: Which observation, on its own, disproves “Every positive integer n can be written as the sum of two different positive integers”?
options: No two different positive integers have sum 2.
The particular pair 2 and 5 does not sum to 6.
questions.explanation: The two smallest distinct positive integers are 1 and 2, so their sum is at least 3. Thus 2 has no permissible representation. A proposed representation that fails does not rule out all others.

questions.stem: Which set refutes “every nonempty finite subset of the integers contains two distinct elements whose sum is even”?
questions.explanation: The only pair in {1,2} has odd sum. The empty set fails the nonempty premise, and the other sets have a same-parity pair.

questions.stem: Which fact is sufficient to refute “for every x>0 there exists y>0 with F(x,y)=0”?
options: A positive x has some negative y with F(x,y)=0.
A positive x has no positive y with F(x,y)=0.
A positive y fails at one positive x.
For every positive x there is a positive y with F(x,y)≠0.
For a negative x there is no y with F(x,y)=0.
questions.explanation: One admissible x must fail for every admissible y. Finding a single failed y is not enough to defeat an existence claim.

questions.stem: To disprove “a function has at most one real zero if its derivative has at most one real zero,” which polynomial suffices?
questions.explanation: The polynomial x(x−1) has two zeros but derivative 2x−1 has only one. The other options have at most one zero each.

questions.stem: A claim states “for every positive integer n, at least one of n − 1 and n + 1 is a prime.” Which listed n disproves it?
questions.explanation: At n = 5 both neighbours, 4 and 6, are composite. Each other offered n has at least one prime neighbour: 3, 2, 3 and 5 respectively.

questions.stem: Which example disproves “if a positive integer is composite, its successor is prime”?
questions.explanation: The composite 8 is followed by 9, which is also composite. The first two n do not meet the premise, and 10,12 are followed by primes.

questions.stem: A student claims: for every integer x between 0 and 11 inclusive there is an integer y in the same range with x + y giving remainder 6 modulo 11 and y < x. Which choice gives an x refuting that claim and also a y that works for the different input x = 6?
questions.explanation: The counterexample is x = 0: no allowed y is less than zero. At the different input x = 6, y = 0 works. A successful witness at one input cannot prove an assertion about every input.

questions.stem: A student claims: for every integer x between 0 and 8 inclusive there is an integer y in the same range with x + y giving remainder 2 modulo 8 and y < x. Which choice gives an x refuting that claim and also a y that works for the different input x = 2?
questions.explanation: The counterexample is x = 0: no allowed y is less than zero. At the different input x = 2, y = 0 works. A successful witness at one input cannot prove an assertion about every input.
